title: Chapter 57: Ashes on Lantern Quay, Part 4 of 5: The Lady's Boy
html:
She did not have a bath.
She went back up the stairs to the Fourth Desk with Gage behind her, and the footman's eyes on her back, and the empty gilt frame with its square of dark red silk at the end of the corridor. And at the top of the last flight, outside the door of the Fourth Desk, she stopped.
Gage stopped behind her.
She stood on the landing for a long moment, with her clean gloved hand on the rail. Looking at nothing. Thinking.
I'd like him found. Gently. Kindly.
She had seen what kindly meant, in the Treasurer's mouth. She had seen it this morning in the Intake Hall, in a black book taken away with no receipt. She had seen it last night, in a locked door in the Fourth Tier rooms, and a careless fellow with a key in his pocket.
She went into the Fourth Desk.
Mister Harrow was at his desk. He looked up as she came in, and then down again, quickly, at his ledger. He had something on his face that she had not seen there before. It took her a moment to know what it was.
He was afraid.
Not of her. For her.
"Miss Elara," he said, very quietly, without looking up. "There is somebody to see you."
She looked down the long room.
There was nobody at her desk. Nobody at the windows. Nobody by the black cupboards.
"Where?"
Mister Harrow did not answer. He moved his eyes. Only his eyes. Toward the far end of the room. Toward her own desk, by the window. And down.
Under it.
The Auditor walked down the long room.
She did not hurry. She walked the way she always walked, between the desks, with her hands at her sides and her boots quiet on the boards. Past Mister Harrow. Past the cupboards with their brass numbers. To her own desk, by her own window, where the Bank's brass scale still stood on the blotter with its brass weights in the right-hand pan and its needle still all the way over at the end of the ivory, trembling a little, the way she had left it.
She stood beside the desk, and did not bend down.
"You can come out," she said.
Nothing happened.
Then, very slowly, something moved in the dark under the desk. In the narrow space between the drawers on the left and the drawers on the right, where her knees went when she sat. Something that had folded itself up very small to fit in there. It unfolded. Carefully. A thin arm. A thin leg. A head, with short dark hair, singed at the ends. And a boy crawled out from under the Auditor's desk on his hands and knees, and knelt on the boards in front of her, and looked up.
She knew him.
Thin. Sharp-faced. Eleven, perhaps, or twelve. His good gray livery was black with soot, and one sleeve of it was burned away to the elbow, and the bare arm under it was wrapped in a strip of white cloth, badly, with a dark stain coming through. His face was gray with ash. His eyes were red. And there was a cut on the ball of his thumb, old and new, the kind of cut you get when you open the same cut again and again.
He had something held against his chest, with both arms. A bundle. Wrapped in a piece of violet cloth. Square, and heavy, by the way he held it.
"Auditor," said the boy.
His voice was hoarse. Smoke-hoarse. And quite steady.
"You lit my way down the kitchen stair," said the Auditor. She did not remember it. But it was in her black book, in her own hand, from two weeks ago: A boy with a candle. Cut thumb. "With a candle."
"Yes, miss."
"You had a cut on your thumb then, too."
"Yes, miss." He did not look at his thumb. "I've always got a cut on my thumb."
She looked at him.
"How did you get in here?"
The boy looked past her, down the long room, at the door. At Gage, who had come in behind her and was standing just inside it, very large, very still, looking at the boy with his small gray eyes.
"He let me," said the boy.
The Auditor turned her head.
Gage did not move. He did not lift his slate. He only stood there by the door, looking at the boy. And then he looked at her, with something in his plain wooden face that she could not read.
"At the second bell," said the boy. "When you went down to the Intake Hall. He came down the stair behind you, and I was on the landing below, in the corner, where the brooms go. I'd been there since the night porter changed. I came in with the coal. Nobody looks at the coal boy." He swallowed. "And he saw me. He looked straight at me. And I thought, that's it, then. And he just—" He stopped. "He just nodded up at this door. And went on down after you."
"And you came in."
"And I came in. And the old gentleman at the desk saw me, and I thought he was going to call out, and he didn't. He went white and he looked at his book." The boy almost smiled. "And I got under there. And I waited. And then you came back and went out again, to the Treasurer, and I stayed. And now you've come back." He looked up at her. "I didn't think you'd come back by yourself."
"I am by myself."
"Yes, miss," said the boy. "I know. That's why I came out."
The Auditor looked down at him for a long moment.
Then she pulled out her chair from the desk, and sat down in it, so that her face was nearer to his. And folded her gloved hands in her lap.
"What's your name?"
"Remy, miss. Remy Castellan."
"Castellan."
"It's not my name. Not really." He shrugged with one shoulder. "It's what she called me. It means the keeper of a castle, Hollis says. Because I kept her doors." He paused. "I don't know what my real name is. Nobody ever told me. I came in a basket."
In a basket.
The Auditor did not say anything.
"The Treasurer wants you found," she said.
"I know." The boy's face did not change. "His men were in her rooms at dawn. In the ash. Turning it over. I watched them from the garden wall. They were looking for these." His arms tightened round the violet bundle. "They didn't find them. Because I had them. I took them at the first lamp, before I went for her." He looked at her. "And they'll want me next. He'll want me. Because I know all the doors."
"So you came here."
"So I came here."
"Why?"
The boy was quiet for a moment.
"Because of what you did," he said. "On the kitchen stair. Two weeks ago. When Gant was taking you down to the cold room to weigh the case. There was blood on the ninth step, where a man had sat. I was holding the candle. And you stopped. And you looked at the blood. And you took your glove off and you touched it. With your bare hand." He looked at her. "And then you put your glove back on and you didn't say anything to Gant. Nothing. You just went on down. And Gant never knew."
The Auditor sat very still.
She did not remember it. Not the stair, or the blood, or touching it. It was two weeks ago. It was gone, fallen away into the long gray nothing where last month and last week and most of yesterday already were.
But she knew she had done it. She knew it the way you know your own handwriting.
"Mrs. Pratt says her kitchen is the only honest room in that house," said Remy. "Was. And I thought, if there's another honest room anywhere, it's the one the lady sits in who touched the blood and didn't tell."
He held out the violet bundle.
He held it out in both arms, kneeling on the boards in front of her chair. Up, toward her. The way the porters held out a lot on a velvet tray. And waited.
The Auditor did not take it.
"What is it?" she said.
"Her books," said Remy. "The real ones. Not the Bourse books. Hers." His voice was very steady. "Seven of them. Back to when she built the cold room. In her hand, mostly. In Hollis's hand, for the last ten years, because her eyes went. What she took. And from who. And when. And who it went to. Every jar." He swallowed. "And there's one more. On top. That's mine."
"Yours."
"I kept it. From when I was ten. In secret. In the coal store, behind a loose brick." He did not look away from her. "What she took, that I saw, or that Hollis told me. And what happened after. I wrote it all down. Because nobody else was going to. And because I thought, one day, somebody will ask. And I want there to be an answer."
The Auditor looked at the bundle in his arms.
At the violet cloth. It was velvet. Old, faded, worn thin at the corners. She knew it. She had seen it last night, hanging in long heavy folds from a brass rail in the gallery of the Memory Bourse. Before it burned.
She took off her right glove.
She did it without thinking. A finger at a time. And laid the glove on the desk beside the brass scale.
Then she reached out and took the bundle out of his arms.
It was heavy. She set it on her knees, and folded back the violet velvet.
There were books inside. Seven big ones, bound in dark leather, worn and old, tied together with a black ribbon. And on top of them, one small one. Very small. The kind of cheap thin notebook a boy could buy for a penny on Quill Row. With a gray paper cover, soft and dirty from handling. And on the gray cover, in pencil, in a boy's careful square hand:
WHAT THE LADY TOOK.
Kept by R. C., from the year he was ten.
The notebook was not tied. It was sealed. A blob of wax had been dripped across the edge of the cover where it met the pages, the way you seal a letter, so that it could not be opened without breaking. Common wax. Red. The cheap kind you buy by the stick. And pressed into the wax, while it was still soft, a seal.
The Auditor bent close to look at it.
It was not the Lady's seal. She knew the Lady's seal. A V, with a crown on it, in violet wax, on every Bourse paper she had ever audited. This was not a V. It was not a letter at all. It was a small round shape, no bigger than her little fingernail, pressed in deep and clean.
A flower.
A small five-petaled flower, open, like a wild rose, or a briar. With a tiny round middle. The kind of flower that grows in hedges, in the country, in the summer, at the edge of long wet fields.
"Where did you get this seal?" said the Auditor.
Remy looked at it.
"It's mine," he said. "It's the only thing that came with me. In the basket." He reached inside the neck of his burned livery shirt, and pulled out a string. And on the string, hanging, small and tarnished and very old, was a ring. A child's ring. Too small for any finger but a baby's. Silver. With a flat round face, and on the face, cut deep and clean, the same small five-petaled flower. "Hollis says it was round my wrist. On a ribbon. When she opened the door." He let it drop back inside his shirt. "I don't know what it means. Nobody ever told me."
The Auditor looked at the flower in the red wax.
She did not know what it meant either.
She looked at it for a long time. Long enough that Mister Harrow, at his desk, stopped writing and looked up. Long enough that Gage, by the door, moved his weight from one foot to the other, and the boards creaked. Long enough that the boy on his knees in front of her chair began to look afraid.
She did not know why her bare hand, resting on the violet velvet, had gone cold. She did not know why, looking at a small five-petaled flower pressed into cheap red wax, she should think of long wet grass, up to her chin, and a hand pulling her along, too fast.
She did not know anything.
She only knew that she had found something. Again.
She took out her black book, and wrote it down.
What the Lady Took
"May I open it?" said the Auditor.
Remy looked at the red wax for a moment. Then he nodded.
"That's what it's for," he said.
She broke the seal with her thumbnail. It came away in two pieces, and the small five-petaled flower split down the middle, and she put the two halves of it on the blotter, side by side, by the brass scale. She did not know why. She did not throw them away.
Then she opened the boy's book.
It was ruled into columns. He had done it himself, with a pencil and the edge of something straight, on every page. Seven columns. And at the top of the first page, in his careful square hand, the headings.
WHO. WHAT. WHEN. FOR WHO. PAID. HOW I KNOW. AFTER.
She read the first line.
Jemmy Ott. His running. Spring, the year I was ten. For the Fennimore boy, who has a bad leg. Paid: forty crowns to the Lady, nothing to Jemmy. I held the lamp. AFTER: Jemmy sits on the Fish Stairs. He can walk. He does not remember why anybody would want to go fast.
The next.
Abel Strand, cooper, his wife. Her voice. Summer. For the Duchess of Ashcombe's daughter, who sings badly. Paid: two hundred crowns. Abel got ten, for the debt. I took the jar up. AFTER: Abel's wife still talks. It doesn't sound like her. Abel says he married a stranger.
The next. And the next.
The Auditor read slowly. She did not skip. She read every line, all the way across, every column. The way she read a ledger. The way she had been taught, or had taught herself, she did not know which. Figure by figure. Word by word.
Halfway down the third page, the hand changed. Not the writer. The pressure. The boy had pressed harder. The pencil had gone into the paper.
Gideon. The Hollow boy. All his feelings, one at a time. Four winters. Jars H.291 to H.340. For the Hill, the Frost Reach, the Choir, for anybody. Paid: nothing. He was owed against his father's debt. I held the lamp, every time. AFTER: Gideon feels nothing. He does not cry. He does not feel the cold. He lives in the arches with Mother Grue. He is my friend. He does not know he is my friend.
And under it:
Big Gideon Hollow, and Saul Hollow, his brother. By agreement. Big Gideon came up on the lift and stood in the dome in front of the Lady and said, Not the boy. Take it out of me. And she did. And Saul said, Me too. And she did. And then she took the boy anyway, for four more winters. Hollis told me. I was too small to hold the lamp yet. AFTER: They turn the drum. They do not know Gideon. They do not know anything.
The Auditor stopped.
She looked up from the page. Out of the window. At the gray river.
She was thinking of a huge barefoot man in a leather apron, carrying a boy up a coal chute on his shoulder. Remy had not told her that. She did not know it. But she thought of it anyway, the way you think of a thing you have dreamed.
She looked down again and read on.
Ned. Bet's brother. Glass thirty-one. From the House of Rest, for the Friday cart. AFTER: Died. He forgot how to swallow.
And beside that, in the AFTER column, very small, in pencil, a drawing. A small five-petaled flower. Open. With a round middle.
The Auditor looked at it.
She turned back. She looked at the other pages. And she saw them now. Here and there, all down the AFTER column. A flower. Small. Drawn with care. Beside a name. And every name with a flower beside it was a name that had died.
Tam Hollin. A line through the name. And a flower.
The Lister girl. A flower.
Old Pask's son. A flower.
"You draw a flower," she said. "For the dead."
Remy was still kneeling on the boards in front of her chair. He had not moved. He was watching her read.
"It's the only thing I've got," he said. "To give them. It's mine. From the basket. I thought, if I've got nothing else, I can give them that." He looked down. "It's not much."
The Auditor did not say anything.
She turned the pages.
She came to Lot 41.
A Lord's Last Evening. A black wood case with a silver clasp. Brought the second Thursday of the month, every month, for a year, by an old harvester, gray to the shoulders, with blue fingers. No name. No pay. He said, Tell your mistress to keep it cold. HOW I KNOW: I opened the door to him. He turned his rod to the left when he put it away. AFTER: Whoever buys it will not live to open it.
And under that, in a different pencil, softer, written fast and small, as if in the dark:
Midwinter. The real one went out by the chute, with the harvester who held up the sky. The other one went out by the garden door, with the Archon's man. I made sure.
The Auditor read it three times.
Then she turned the page.
And on the next page, at the top, by itself, there was an entry with no line ruled above it. As if the boy had started a new page for it on purpose. As if it did not belong with the others.
The pink one.
WHO: Not known. A girl. Young. WHAT: Her laugh. When she was small. Laughing in a field, being chased. WHEN: Spring. Six winters ago. The Thaw month. FOR WHO: Nobody. The Lady bought it to keep. PAID: A great deal. More than for anything else I ever saw. HOW I KNOW: I was five. I was under the table. The Lady said I must never tell. She is dead now, so I am telling.
The Auditor's bare hand lay very still on the page.
She read on.
It came from the Bank. From the Fourth Desk. A man brought it, in the night, from the Fourth Desk, with a paper. The paper was signed with one letter. The Lady said to Hollis, after he had gone: It is the only thing in this house that was given away for love. Not sold. Not taken. Given. She would never tell me what she meant. She kept it on her table, in the little silver rack, always, with a pink ribbon on it. She held it to her ear sometimes, at night, when she couldn't sleep.
AFTER: Midwinter, in the fire, the Inquisitor walked across the floor and took it off her table. Only that one. He held it to his ear. I saw him from the stair. Then he put it in his coat and went away.
There was no flower beside it.
The Auditor sat at her desk by her window on the third floor of the Oblivion Bank, with the boy's book open on her knees and her bare right hand flat on the page, and did not move.
A girl. Young. Her laugh. Laughing in a field, being chased.
Six winters ago. The Thaw month.
From the Fourth Desk. Signed with one letter.
She did not have to ask what letter.
She did not use the Sight. She did not need to. She could feel it anyway, under her bare palm, coming up out of the cheap thin paper of a boy's penny notebook the way cold comes up out of stone. Not a lie. The other thing. The thing she had felt only once before, in the cold room, on the Thursday before last, with her bare hand on the black wood of a case. Something folded. Folded very small, and very tight, and held.
Given away for love.
She had been in a field. In long wet grass, up to her chin. With a boy's hand pulling hers, too fast. Come on, Ellie. Keep up. Don't let go. And she had been laughing. She had heard it last night, in the white light, for a hundred breaths. Her own laugh.
And then it had gone.
And on the morning of the ninth of the Thaw month, six years ago, she had woken up in a narrow bed at the top of the Bank with no memory of anything, and a giant on a stool by the door with a slate.
And she had never laughed since.
And somewhere, in the same spring, in the night, a man had carried a small glass vial from the Fourth Desk to the Memory Bourse, with a paper signed with one letter. And the Lady had paid more for it than for anything else in forty years. And tied a pink ribbon round it. And kept it on her table, and held it to her ear at night when she could not sleep.
And last night, in the fire, Silas Kross had walked across the burning floor of the dome and taken it, and held it to his ear, and put it in his coat.
The Inquisitor's orders. She's not to be held.
The Auditor shut the book.
She shut it very gently. The way you shut a door on a sleeping child. And laid her bare hand flat on the gray paper cover, over the boy's careful square letters. WHAT THE LADY TOOK. And sat there.
She was not crying. She noticed that. She had cried last night, in the kitchen passage, for the first time in six years, and she was not crying now. She felt quite calm. Quite cold. The way she felt when she had found the lie in a ledger, and knew the figure, and had only to write it down.
She did not know the figure. Not yet.
But she knew there was one.
"Gage," she said.
She did not raise her voice. She did not turn round. But she heard the boards creak by the door, and the great soft boots come down the long room toward her, between the desks, and stop beside her chair.
She did not look up at him.
"Did you know?" she said.
The chalk did not move.
There was a long silence in the Fourth Desk. Mister Harrow had stopped writing again. The ash went past the window, very fine, very slow.
Then the chalk scratched on the slate. Slowly. A long time. Longer than she had ever heard him write.
He held it down beside her, by the window, in the gray light.
I was there. You asked me to take it. You said, Take it somewhere it will be kept, and never tell me. I said I would not tell you. I have not told you.
And under it, smaller, squeezed in at the bottom of the slate:
You did not ask me not to tell you who.
The Auditor read it.
She read it twice.
Then she looked up at Gage. At the plain wooden face, very high above her, with the gray light on it. At the small gray eyes.
"Who?" she said. "Who did I give it for?"
Gage looked down at her for a long moment.
Then he wiped the slate. And did not write anything. And let it hang on its cord against his chest, blank.
And lifted his great hand, slowly, and put it on her head. On her short dark hair, coming down at one side, gray with ash. Just for a moment. The way you put your hand on the head of a child who has asked a question you are not allowed to answer yet.
Then he took it away.
She understood.
Not the answer. Not who. But that he would tell her. Some day. When it was time. And that it was not yet. And that he was sorry.
Not yet. He had written that on his slate once, in the autumn. She had it in her black book. Not yet. He is listening.
She looked down at the boy.
Remy was still kneeling on the boards by her chair. He had watched all of it. Gage's slate. Her face. He had not said a word. His sharp face under the ash was very white.
"Remy," said the Auditor.
"Yes, miss."
"The Treasurer wants you found. And whatever you are carrying. He wants the Fourth Desk to keep it for him, under clause eleven, until he can come and see it."
The boy went still.
"So I will keep it," said the Auditor. "Under clause eleven."
She stood up. She went to the black cupboards along the inside wall. To the one with the brass number 11 on its door. She took a key from the chain round her neck, under her collar, and unlocked it, and opened it.
It was a deep cupboard. Deeper than it looked. Shelves at the top, with the vellum of the Charter on them, rolled, in a leather case. And below the shelves, a space. Tall enough for a boy to sit in. Dark. Dry. With a smell of old paper and cedar.
"The Charter says," said the Auditor, "that whatever the Fourth Desk holds under clause eleven may not be looked at, or touched, or taken, by anybody but the Auditor. Not the Council. Not the Treasurer. Not the Archon himself." She looked at Remy. "Whose record shall stand."
Remy looked at the cupboard.
Then he looked at her.
And then, without a word, he got up off his knees, and took the seven dark leather books in their violet velvet, and his own small gray one, and climbed into the cupboard under the shelves with them, and sat down, with his knees drawn up and the books in his lap. And looked up at her out of the dark.
"Is there a clause for this?" he said.
And the Auditor of the Fourth Desk heard herself say what she had said in the Intake Hall, three bells ago, to a man with a full glass of brandy.
"There is now."
She shut the door, gently, and did not lock it. And put the key back on its chain, under her collar. And turned round.
Mister Harrow was looking at her from his desk. Gage was looking at her from beside her chair.
"Mister Harrow," she said. "Please write in the day book: Cupboard eleven. Held under audit. Contents not to be listed."
Mister Harrow dipped his pen.
"Yes, Miss Elara," he said. And wrote it. And blotted it.
And then, for the first time in twenty-two years, so far as the Auditor knew, Mister Harrow of the Fourth Desk asked a question.
"Will there be anything else, Miss?"
The Auditor looked out of the window. At Lantern Quay. At the gray river. At the gray ash falling.
"Yes," she said. "Fetch my coat. I have to go to Ferrule Street."
